Connector Documentation Automation

Automated documentation generation for 400+ security integrations by building a source-driven pipeline from connector YAML metadata, saving an estimated 40-60+ person-months of manual effort.

AutomationPythonYAMLDocs-as-CodeScale

Problem

The security automation platform supported 400+ third-party integrations (connectors), but documentation for these connectors was:

  • Manually created and maintained, leading to inconsistencies across the catalog
  • Frequently out of sync with the actual connector behavior and configuration
  • Missing standardized authentication and configuration guides for many connectors
  • Impossible to scale with a single-person documentation team

At the rate of manual authoring, covering the full connector catalog would have required an estimated 40-60+ person-months of effort.

My Role

I designed and executed the entire connector documentation automation program: content modeling, pipeline development, guide creation, validation, and publishing integration.

What I Did

  1. Designed the content model by analyzing connector repository structure and identifying the source files that define each connector's metadata, configuration parameters, and action definitions
  2. Built a conversion pipeline (Python) that generates a standardized Markdown documentation page per connector from:
    • connector.yaml for metadata and keywords
    • Configuration asset YAML files for setup parameters
    • Action YAML files for input/output parameter tables
    • README content for connector overview
  3. Created authentication and configuration guides at scale, delivering 40+ authentication guides and 59 configuration guides to improve connector onboarding
  4. Built validation tooling to enforce publishing platform constraints (heading depth, table sizes, content length) and catch formatting risks before ingestion
  5. Hardened changelog and release automation by identifying failure modes in the existing release/publish workflows and implementing fallback-safe patterns
  6. Produced operational runbooks for triggering updates, verifying output, troubleshooting failures, and onboarding new team members

Constraints

  • 400+ connector repositories across a GitHub organization, each with slightly different structures
  • Publishing platform (Archbee) had specific ingestion limits that required content shaping
  • Connector releases continued independently; documentation had to stay synchronized without manual intervention
  • No dedicated engineering support for the pipeline; built and maintained entirely within the documentation team

Outcomes

Customer Impact

  • Standardized documentation across the full connector catalog, reducing customer confusion during integration setup
  • Expanded authentication guide coverage improved onboarding success for new connector adoption
  • Reduced documentation drift by keeping docs synchronized with live connector source definitions

Operational Impact

  • Saved an estimated 40-60+ person-months of manual documentation effort
  • Established a repeatable pipeline that scales with the connector catalog growth
  • Reduced release-time documentation bottlenecks with automated changelog and doc update workflows
  • Produced reusable process documentation for demos, onboarding, and team handoffs

Technical Approach (Highlights)

  • Flattened nested configuration schemas using dot notation for readability
  • Generated consistent input/output parameter tables with real examples from YAML where available
  • Applied safe defaults when descriptions or examples were missing in source files
  • Parallelized bulk conversion for performance across hundreds of repositories
  • Used shallow clone and marketplace-based filtering to process only published connectors

Lessons Learned

  • Source-driven documentation scales; manual documentation does not. Making the connector repository the single source of truth was the most important architectural decision
  • Validation tooling pays for itself immediately: catching format issues before publishing prevents customer-visible broken pages
  • Operational runbooks are as important as the automation itself; without them, the pipeline becomes a single point of failure tied to one person
